doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Playing on top of or behind the beat; Ray Brown and drummers
summary: Ray Brown's lesson on giving the beat an edge, dealing with rushing or laid-back drummers, and keeping tempo for the horn players.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well I think about that less and less. I thought about it when I was younger and when I had a lesson with Ray Brown, who was known for playing on top of the beat so to speak, or other musicians would say he played really on top of the beat. When I asked Ray about it Ray was like well, he said, “I like to give the music an edge but I don’t like it to get too fast, but I like it to have an edge.” So he liked to really propel the beat I think, you know what I mean? Whether you call that top of the beat or whatever. And, you know, I don’t like to think about it. Because I think what happens is when you are a freelancer in these days there are very few bands where you’re playing with the same person all the time you know. So if you’re a freelancer you’re going to get some drummers that really play very laid back, which gives you a little more authority to play. The two things, you just don’t want it to speed up and you don’t want it to slow down. So you have to kind of find — you know if the drummer plays so far back well then you’ve got to really push the beat, you know what I mean? Because otherwise it’s going to drag. If the drummer is rushing and — I find it harder to play with the rushing drummer, and I have to think about this when I’m booking my own gigs, you know what I mean? If I’m trying to play a note, I’m singing more, I don’t want a drummer that’s pushing the beat too much because I’m trying to like, you know, keep it there. And so that’s even harder because you’ve really got to put the anchor on their beat, and that takes a lot of concentration too. So it really depends on who you’re playing with, this on top of the beat, behind the beat. The main thing is the horn player wants you to keep it at the tempo that it was kind of off at, or somewhere in there, because they’ve got to play the head on the way in and they’ve got to play the head on the way out. If it gets too fast for them to play the head out, they’re not exactly happy with the rhythm section then are they? So it’s really, like for me it’s a responsibility of keeping the time within a reasonable — you know if it’s kind of there [snaps fingers] it’s your job as a bass player, to keep it around there. And I find the best musicians really do that, you know what I mean? And so that’s why you don’t even think about it with great drummers and great piano players. It just flows. Because everybody knows where the beat is and it’s just — I had one of those nights the other night. You know I played with a drummer for the first time, and it’s just so nice when you hear the beat exactly the same place. And he was trying all kinds of stuff on the drums. Alvin Atkinson. Wonderful. He was just going for it. And the gig had this lovely looseness, so it was like yeah, just go for it. But it was always, when we came back in to play it was always just there.
